title: Toxic underground fires spreading at California landfills
excerpt: LOS ANGELES -- Three years ago, environmental regulators discovered garbage burning deep inside the Chiquita Canyon Landfill in the Santa Clarita Valley. Few imagined the calamity that would follow.
content_html:
LOS ANGELES -- Three years ago, environmental regulators discovered garbage burning deep inside the Chiquita Canyon Landfill in the Santa Clarita Valley. Few imagined the calamity that would follow.

Somehow the landfill's pollution control system introduced oxygen below, causing decades-old waste to rapidly decompose, generating intense heat and eventually widespread smoldering, federal and state environmental agencies say.

The broiling temperatures released toxic gases and hazardous liquid waste that bubbled up to the surface. Residents living in the nearby communities of Val Verde and Castaic have phoned in thousands of complaints about stench and lived with nausea, dizziness and trouble breathing.

The underground fire has tripled in size since first confirmed in 2023. Recently a towering mound of landfill garbage perched on the hillside has warped and threatens to trigger an avalanche of garbage and chemical-filled liquid, or leachate, according to the California water board. Waste Connections, the landfill's owner and operator, says it has been working to stabilize that area.

"In a worst case scenario, the hillside can liquefy and actually slide into the community," Assembly member Pilar Schiavo, D-Santa Clarita, said at a news conference last month.

At first, local officials described the problem in Los Angeles County at Chiquita Canyon landfill as a rare, even unprecedented disaster. But since then, California regulators have learned that at least two other landfills are wrestling with high temperatures and similar conditions.

Scorching temperatures have overtaken at least 30 acres of El Sobrante landfill near Corona in Riverside County. Excessive heat and emissions have also been detected at Avenal landfill in the San Joaquin Valley.

The discoveries raise an unsettling question: How many landfills are dealing with these disasters? Are they a broader problem in California?

At Chiquita Canyon, conditions have continued to deteriorate.

Some residents have taken extreme measures to escape the toxic pollution. They've worn gas masks and slept overnight in grocery store parking lots. Several families sold their homes.

Those who have stayed continue to deal with risks to their health and safety. Schiavo said the stench near Chiquita Canyon has gotten worse in recent days as workers try to stabilize the hillside.

In Val Verde, children out of school for the summer have hardly been able to enjoy their time off.

"They are already suffering -- prisoners in their own homes," Schiavo said. "They have a great trampoline in front of their house. They can't jump around on because of this toxic air."

On a recent weekday morning, landfill workers were staged around the damaged, western side of the landfill with heavy machinery. Across the street, dozens Los Angeles County firefighter recruits jogged at the Del Valle Regional Training Center, pushing through the inescapable aroma of trash in the air.

Abigail DeSesa, a longtime resident of Val Verde who lives about a mile from Chiquita Canyon, said she regularly wakes up with pounding headaches she believes are related to landfill gases from the fire. She's gone to a community relief center set up at a local hotel to escape the smell, but has to return home at the end of the day.

"The gas is getting into our homes and I am waking up sick every morning," DeSesa said. "Where is the relief for that? I did not break the landfill, so why am I paying a heavy price with my physical and mental health to fix it?"

Chiquita Canyon closed at the end of the 2024 and stopped accepting new garbage. But the fire is expected to last for years as it continues to consume decades-old trash.

Underground landfill fires are complex, nearly impossible to extinguish once they break out. As regulators search for a solution, residents find themselves struggling with the wait.

content_html_zh:
洛杉矶——三年前，环境监管机构发现圣克拉丽塔山谷奇基塔峡谷垃圾填埋场深处正在燃烧垃圾。 很少有人想象到随之而来的灾难。

联邦和州环境机构表示，不知何故，垃圾填埋场的污染控制系统将氧气引入下方，导致几十年前的废物迅速分解，产生强烈的热量，最终导致大面积阴燃。

炽热的温度释放出有毒气体和危险的液体废物，这些废物冒出地表。 居住在 Val Verde 和 Castaic 附近社区的居民接到了数千起有关恶臭的投诉电话，并感到恶心、头晕和呼吸困难。

自 2023 年首次确认以来，地下火灾规模已扩大两倍。 据加州水务局称，最近，山坡上的一座高耸的垃圾填埋场已经变形，有可能引发垃圾和化学填充液体或渗滤液的雪崩。 垃圾填埋场的所有者和运营商废物连接公司表示，他们一直在努力稳定该地区的局势。

“在最坏的情况下，山坡可能会液化并滑入社区，”圣克拉里塔州议员皮拉尔·夏沃 (Pilar Schiavo) 在上个月的新闻发布会上表示。

起初，当地官员将洛杉矶县奇基塔峡谷垃圾填埋场的问题描述为一场罕见的、甚至是史无前例的灾难。 但从那时起，加州监管机构了解到，至少还有另外两个垃圾填埋场正在与高温和类似的条件作斗争。

河滨县科罗纳附近的 El Sobrante 垃圾填埋场，至少 30 英亩的土地都遭遇了酷热的天气。 圣华金河谷的阿维纳尔垃圾填埋场也检测到过多的热量和排放。

这些发现提出了一个令人不安的问题：有多少垃圾填埋场正在应对这些灾难？ 它们是加州更广泛的问题吗？

在奇基塔峡谷，情况继续恶化。

一些居民采取了极端措施来躲避有毒污染。 他们戴着防毒面具，在杂货店停车场过夜。 几个家庭卖掉了他们的房子。

那些留下来的人继续应对健康和安全风险。 夏沃说，最近几天，随着工人们试图稳定山坡，奇基塔峡谷附近的恶臭变得更加严重。

在Val Verde，暑假失学的孩子们几乎无法享受假期。

“他们已经在受苦——被关在自己家里，”夏沃说。 “他们家门前有一个很棒的蹦床。 由于空气有毒，他们无法跳来跳去。”

最近一个工作日的早上，垃圾填埋场工人带着重型机械在受损的垃圾填埋场西侧周围驻扎。 街对面，数十名洛杉矶县消防员新兵在德尔瓦勒地区培训中心慢跑，穿过空气中不可避免的垃圾气味。

阿比盖尔·德塞萨 (Abigail DeSesa) 是瓦尔维德 (Val Verde) 的长期居民，住在距离奇基塔峡谷 (Chiquita Canyon) 约一英里的地方。她说，她经常醒来时感到剧烈头痛，她认为这与垃圾填埋场火灾产生的气体有关。 为了躲避这种气味，她去了当地一家酒店设立的社区救济中心，但最终还是不得不回家。

“气体正在进入我们的家，我每天早上醒来都会感到恶心，”德塞萨说。 “哪里可以得到缓解呢？ 我没有破坏垃圾填埋场，为什么我要用我的身心健康付出沉重的代价来修复它呢？”

Chiquita Canyon 于 2024 年底关闭，并停止接收新垃圾。 但大火预计将持续数年，因为它继续消耗数十年的垃圾。

地下垃圾填埋场火灾十分复杂，一旦爆发几乎不可能扑灭。 当监管机构寻求解决方案时，居民发现自己在等待中苦苦挣扎。
